the_trap_and_the_fix.whatItWas: check.mjs:154 hardcoded `const OPR_RE = /\bOPR-[A-Za-z0-9]+/g`, a hand-written second implementation of the declared format. In `FL-OPR-01` the `\b` sits before `OPR` (the hyphen is not a word character), so it extracted the truncated `OPR-01` and failed it against the namespaced format: an extraction bug that reads as a defective board.
the_trap_and_the_fix.whatItIsNow: _design/smartcity-fleet-lens/check.mjs:122-145 -- formatBody()/stemFrom()/sampleFrom()/candidateReFor() derive the extractor and every fixture from the DECLARED format's own body. The candidate is the maximal hyphen-and-alphanumeric token carrying the stem, never a prefix of it, and it is deliberately WIDER than the format: a predicate that refuses references outside the format must be able to SEE one, and an extractor as strict as the format would pass over a bare `OPR-01` silently.
the_trap_and_the_fix.the_widening_defended: The tail of the candidate pattern is `+`, not `*`, so a lone stem -- how a board DESCRIBES the format in prose ('declared format: OPR- followed by exactly two digits') -- is not treated as a reference. That case is a self-test.

LESSON: A browser probe is only as honest as what it does when a gesture fails. Wrapping driver calls in `.catch(() => {})` makes an unreachable control and a control that never fired produce the same artifact: nothing. Record each gesture's outcome and its error.

A gesture that did not THROW is not a gesture that WORKED. `form.requestSubmit()` returned cleanly while the field was empty and no request ever left the page. Believe a driven search only when the request it should cause arrives, from the frame that was driven.

When a UI control refuses a pointer with 'Element is not visible' in EVERY dock mode, stop re-trying and read the page's own CSS: the product may be hiding it deliberately when embedded. The failing click was the clue that found `pm-embedded`, and without that read the probe would have reported a product defect that is a design decision.
